clue.text: A name to prize in entertainment

definitions.meaning: a boy's forename, as borne by the writer Wilde
the Academy Award statuette given in the film world

explanation.definitionFit: It is both a common forename and the nickname of the film industry's Academy Award statuette.

clue.text: How can one get even with these members of society ?

definitions.text: How can one get even with these members of society ?

parts.words: How can one get even with these members of society ?
parts.note: plays on odd versus even: members of a friendly society whose name says they are uneven chaps

explanation.walkthrough: 'Get even' suggests revenge, but plays on odd and even. The Oddfellows are a British friendly society, a mutual-aid club.
explanation.definitionFit: Members of the Independent Order of the mutual-aid fraternity founded in England.

clue.text: Poetry's ragged robin

definitions.meaning: Thomas ..., the Elizabethan poet and songwriter
a pink wild flower of damp meadows

explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Campion was an English poet, and ragged robin is a pink-flowered plant of the same genus as the red and white varieties of this wildflower.

clue.text: Like accommodation offered for swinging cats

definitions.text: Like accommodation offered for swinging cats

parts.words: Like accommodation offered for swinging cats
parts.note: draws on the saying 'no room to swing a cat' for a cramped place: here there is plenty

explanation.walkthrough: The saying 'not enough room to swing a cat' describes a tiny space; lodgings where cats can be swung are spacious.
explanation.definitionFit: Spacious lodgings have plenty of space inside.

clue.text: Do they do the rounds of the clubs ?

definitions.text: Do they do the rounds of the clubs ?

parts.words: Do they do the rounds of the clubs ?
parts.note: suggests drinkers on a pub crawl or golfers, but means members of a service club whose emblem is a wheel and whose meetings rotate

explanation.walkthrough: The Rotary Club got its name because early meetings rotated between members' offices; its emblem is a wheel, so its members 'do the rounds' of their clubs.
explanation.definitionFit: Members of Rotary International belong to local clubs whose name and wheel badge come from rotation.

clue.text: I used rum, but somehow left this

definitions.note: the clue speaks of the thing left behind, a noun for what remains

indicators.note: says the letters of the preceding words are worked into some other order

explanation.surface: A drinker confesses that rum was used and something remained.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters of I USED RUM are rearranged, as 'somehow' signals. 'But' only joins.
explanation.definitionFit: A residuum is the remainder or residue after a process such as evaporation.

clue.text: Deal, perhaps, that gets a doctor into a row

indicators.note: the doctor's letters go inside the row's letters

parts.note: a tier is a row, as of seats
MB is Bachelor of Medicine, a British medical degree

explanation.surface: A card game deal that seats a physician in a line of players.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Deal' is not handing out cards but deal wood, sawn pine or fir planks; 'perhaps' marks it as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: Deal is a kind of softwood, so it is one example of cut wood for building.

clue.text: Tale-tellings in the family ?

definitions.meaning: narrations or accounts, as in relating a story
kin, people related by blood or marriage

explanation.definitionFit: The word means both narratives of events and members of one's kin.

clue.text: Theirs is not a colourless existence

definitions.text: Theirs is not a colourless existence

parts.words: Theirs is not a colourless existence
parts.note: sounds like praise for a lively life, but means painters whose work is full of paint

explanation.walkthrough: 'Colourless' suggests dull; literally these people live surrounded by colour.
explanation.definitionFit: Painters work with colours every day.

clue.text: Playwright who got a kick out of a trifle

definitions.text: Playwright who got a kick out of a trifle

parts.words: Playwright who got a kick out of a trifle
parts.note: the Irish dramatist George Bernard, whose surname is the dismissive cry ... at a trifle minus its opening letter

explanation.walkthrough: 'Pshaw!' is an exclamation brushing aside a trifle; take the P out and the playwright remains. The setter gives no clear signal for losing the P, so this reads as a cryptic definition.
explanation.definitionFit: George Bernard of that surname was the Irish playwright of Pygmalion.

clue.text: Children who follow one parent get the plums

indicators.note: the children's word comes after the parent's word, so it is placed second

parts.note: a dam is a mother, used of animals
sons are male children

explanation.surface: Kids siding with one parent are rewarded with the best bits.
explanation.definitionFit: Damsons are a small dark variety of plum.

clue.text: Wherein John Citizen undertook private duties

definitions.text: Wherein John Citizen undertook private duties

parts.words: Wherein John Citizen undertook private duties
parts.note: the ordinary citizen serving as a 'private', the lowest army rank, in a part-time citizen force

explanation.walkthrough: 'Private duties' sounds like personal business, but a private is a common soldier; John Citizen is the ordinary man who joins a citizen army.
explanation.definitionFit: A militia is a body of civilians trained as soldiers for emergencies.

clue.text: I'm back in one of the British Isles with a girl !

indicators.note: the turned letters are placed inside the island's name

parts.note: the Isle of Ely, an old name for the fenland district around the cathedral city in Cambridgeshire

indicators.note: the contraction is read from right to left

parts.note: the contraction taken as its letters

explanation.surface: A traveller announces a return to a British island in a woman's company.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns IM into MI, which goes inside ELY. The Isle of Ely is not a real island but a raised area of the Cambridgeshire Fens.
explanation.definitionFit: A common female forename.

clue.text: Not a singular performer

parts.note: reads as 'not remarkable', but means one who sings or plays as one of a pair, never alone

explanation.walkthrough: 'Singular' looks like 'outstanding'; here it means single, so the performer always has a partner.
explanation.definitionFit: This musician performs only in duets, works for two players or voices.

clue.text: Hot cake — containing the finest wine, we hear ?

indicators.note: the phrase meaning the top wine store is spoken aloud and matched by its sound

parts.note: a best cellar would hold the choicest wines

explanation.surface: A warm pastry filled with top-quality wine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hot cake' comes from 'selling like hot cakes'; a best cellar, holding the finest wine, sounds like the word for a fast-selling book.
explanation.definitionFit: Something selling like hot cakes is a book or product in huge demand.

clue.text: Proud and stubborn beasts in a mix-up on the floor

indicators.note: the two animals' names are jumbled together into a new order

parts.note: the lion is the proud beast, 'beasts' applying to both words
the mule is the proverbially stubborn animal

explanation.surface: Two zoo creatures end up in a tangle on the ground.
explanation.walkthrough: LION and MULE together are rearranged, as signalled by 'in a mix-up'. 'Beasts' covers both adjectives: the proud beast and the stubborn one.
explanation.definitionFit: Lino is a hard-wearing sheet covering laid on floors.

clue.text: There is a pronounced difference in these

definitions.text: There is a pronounced difference in these

parts.words: There is a pronounced difference in these
parts.note: 'pronounced' reads as 'marked', but means spoken: tongues differ in how they are said

explanation.walkthrough: 'Pronounced difference' seems to mean a big gap; read literally it is a difference in speech, as between French and German.
explanation.definitionFit: Tongues of different peoples differ in what is spoken.

clue.text: Make us some sweet dish

indicators.note: used as 'make into', the letters of the next two words are formed into something new

explanation.surface: A request for someone to prepare a dessert for the group.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Make' reads as 'cook', but it signals rearranging the letters of US SOME.
explanation.definitionFit: A mousse is a light whipped dessert, often chocolate.

clue.text: This dealer has a handle to his name and takes outside credit

indicators.note: the credit's letters go round the outside of the name's letters

parts.note: CR is the accounting abbreviation for credit
a handle is slang for a name or title

explanation.surface: A merchant with a title to his name also offers external credit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Has a handle to his name' sounds like a title such as Sir; 'takes outside' puts C and R either side of HANDLE.
explanation.definitionFit: A chandler is a dealer in candles or in ships' supplies.

clue.text: Shaking, and this, changed Red Queen into Black Kitten

definitions.text: Shaking, and this, changed Red Queen into Black Kitten

parts.words: Shaking, and this, changed Red Queen into Black Kitten
parts.note: refers to the two short chapters near the end of Through the Looking-Glass in which Alice shakes the Red Queen and then finds herself holding her black kitten

explanation.walkthrough: In Lewis Carroll's Through the Looking-Glass, chapter 10 is 'Shaking' and chapter 11 is the one-line chapter in which Alice comes to, and the Red Queen has become the kitten.
explanation.definitionFit: Rousing from sleep is what turns Alice's dream queen back into her real pet.

clue.text: Once a VI.P. by the Nile ; with a bit of luck he dives in

definitions.text: Once a VI.P. by the Nile

indicators.note: the answer sits inside the run of letters across these words

explanation.surface: An Egyptian notable plunges into the river hoping for good fortune.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With a bit of luck' looks like a hope, but the letters run on from 'luck' into 'he dives'. The Khedive was the viceroy of Egypt under Ottoman rule.
explanation.definitionFit: The Khedive was the Ottoman viceroy ruling Egypt from 1867 to 1914.

clue.text: That old, old, story !

parts.note: the weary cry at a tale or joke heard too many times

explanation.walkthrough: The word is also a tree and a conker; here only its sense of a stale, repeated anecdote applies.
explanation.definitionFit: A stale joke or anecdote told over and over is known by this nut's name.

clue.text: Breathing space

parts.note: usually a short rest, here read literally as an opening the air passes through

explanation.walkthrough: 'Breathing space' normally means a pause; literally it is a passage for breath in the nose.
explanation.definitionFit: Each opening in the nose through which air is drawn in.

clue.text: Beauty consultant went to the wall

definitions.text: Beauty consultant went to the wall

parts.words: Beauty consultant went to the wall
parts.note: 'went to the wall' means failed in business, but the fairy-tale Queen consulted the looking-glass on the wall about beauty

explanation.walkthrough: In Snow White the Queen asks the one on the wall who is the fairest of all; 'went to the wall' also suggests a business failing.
explanation.definitionFit: A looking-glass is consulted about one's appearance and often hangs on a wall.

clue.text: A copper takes evasive action, just to deceive

definitions.note: a verb phrase standing for the noun: the act of deceiving or what deceives

parts.note: d was the abbreviation for an old penny, a copper coin
eluding, the act of escaping or evading

explanation.surface: A policeman dodges and weaves simply to trick someone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Copper' suggests a policeman, but here it is the penny coin, D from the Latin denarius in pre-decimal British money; 'takes' just joins it to ELUSION.
explanation.definitionFit: A false belief or the act of misleading, a deception imposed on the mind.

clue.text: Article on Man, perhaps, that divides the Church

parts.note: a is the indefinite article
the Isle of Man is an example of an island in the Irish Sea

explanation.surface: An essay about humanity which causes a split in the church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Man' is not humanity but the Isle of Man, a self-governing island between Britain and Ireland; 'perhaps' shows it is one example of an island.
explanation.definitionFit: The passage running between the pews splits a church's seating in two.

clue.text: Book for a picture show

parts.note: suggests booking cinema seats, but means a volume for displaying photographs

explanation.walkthrough: 'Book' looks like a verb (reserve), but it is a noun: a book of pictures.
explanation.definitionFit: A bound book for keeping and displaying photographs or stamps.

clue.text: The ultimate in, snobbery?

definitions.meaning: a snob was once a cobbler, and shoemaking uses a foot-shaped wooden form

explanation.walkthrough: 'Snob' is an old word for a shoemaker; snobbery here is the cobbler's trade, which uses a wooden foot model.
explanation.definitionFit: It means final, and is also the cobbler's foot-shaped mould.

clue.text: One takes a different bearing to arrive here

definitions.text: One takes a different bearing to arrive here

indicators.note: the word bearing is to be taken in another form, its letters rearranged

explanation.surface: A navigator alters course to reach the destination.
explanation.walkthrough: A rearranged 'bearing' gives the destination: Abinger is a village in Surrey, England.
explanation.definitionFit: This Surrey village is the place reached by rearranging the given bearing.

clue.text: No mean party ?

parts.note: reads as a lavish celebration, but describes a generous person and a British political party at once

explanation.walkthrough: 'Mean' is stingy and 'party' a political grouping: the word means generous and names Britain's old Liberal Party.
explanation.definitionFit: Generous, not stingy, and also the name of a British political party.

clue.text: He's expected to take notes

parts.note: suggests a secretary writing minutes, but the notes are banknotes held for a club or society

explanation.walkthrough: 'Notes' sounds like written jottings; it means money taken in and kept by the officer in charge of the funds.
explanation.definitionFit: The officer who looks after an organisation's money collects and holds its cash.

clue.text: It's held at the back, by gum

definitions.text: It's held at the back, by gum

parts.words: It's held at the back, by gum
parts.note: 'by gum' sounds like a mild northern English oath, but literally the gum holds a back grinding tooth

explanation.walkthrough: 'By gum!' is a dated northern English exclamation; read literally it says the gums hold this tooth at the back of the mouth.
explanation.definitionFit: A back tooth for grinding food, set in the gum.
